Q223.t: An island that is mostly one enormous dome of ice
Q223.s: On flights between Europe and North America you often cross an island that is almost all ice. The ice sheet covers about four-fifths of Greenland and is up to 3 km thick, so its crest sits more than 3,000 m above the sea. At the edges, dark peaks and fjords break through, and in summer the ice is freckled with turquoise meltwater lakes.
Q223.w: A vast featureless white plateau, edged by dark mountains, deep fjords and icebergs drifting off the coast.
f: Greenland is the world's largest island, about 2.2 million km² — roughly four times the size of France.
If all its ice melted, the world's oceans would rise by about 7 metres.
Only about 56,000 people live here, nearly all on the ice-free coast.

q.q: What share of Greenland is covered by its ice sheet?

Q35942.t: Thousands of kilometres of ocean, stitched with atolls
Q35942.s: From the air it is mostly deep blue, broken now and then by a ring of turquoise — an atoll — or the green ridges of a volcanic island. Polynesia is a vast triangle with Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island at its corners. People settled all of it in canoes, reading stars, swells and birds, long before Europeans arrived.
Q35942.w: Scattered turquoise rings of reef with pale lagoons, and now and then a dark-green volcanic peak wrapped in cloud.
f: The name comes from the Greek for 'many islands'.
New Zealand, the triangle's south-western corner, was settled only about 700 years ago — one of the last large lands people reached.
Polynesian languages are so close that 'moana', the ocean, is the same word in Hawaii and New Zealand.

q.q: Which island marks a corner of the Polynesian Triangle?

Q669037.t: Columbus's mistaken 'Indies', strung across turquoise seas
Q669037.s: The islands curve for thousands of kilometres from the Bahamas and Cuba to Trinidad, and from above the colours give them away: shallow banks glowing turquoise, white sand, green mountains. The name is an old mistake — Columbus believed he had reached the Indies of Asia when he landed here in 1492. The big islands lie to the west; a chain of small volcanic ones closes off the Caribbean to the east.
Q669037.w: Big mountainous islands to the west, a curving chain of small volcanic ones to the east, bright turquoise shallows in between.
f: The highest peak, Pico Duarte on Hispaniola, rises to about 3,100 m.
The Caribbean Sea takes its name from the Caribs, a people of the Lesser Antilles.

q.q: On which island is the highest peak of the West Indies?

Q928.t: More than 7,000 islands, reefs and volcano cones
Q928.s: Green, mountainous islands break the sea into straits and bays, each coast fringed with a pale line of reef. There are more than 7,000 of them, though Luzon in the north and Mindanao in the south hold over two-thirds of the land. The archipelago sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, so look for volcanic cones and crater lakes among the forested ridges.
Q928.w: A maze of green islands and narrow straits, with pale reef edges along the coasts.
f: The islands were named in the 1540s after Prince Philip of Spain, later King Philip II.
On Bohol more than 1,200 rounded hills turn brown in the dry season — the famous Chocolate Hills.
The Philippines lies in the Coral Triangle, the region with the richest variety of reef life on Earth.

q.q: Which Spanish king gave his name to the Philippines?

Q17.t: A 3,000-km arc of mountains rising from the Pacific
Q17.s: From cruise height Japan is a long, crumpled arc of forested mountains, with cities squeezed onto the narrow plains between the slopes and the sea. Four big islands carry almost everyone, and thousands of smaller ones are scattered around them. At night the Pacific coast from Tokyo to Osaka glows as one nearly unbroken ribbon of light.
Q17.w: Rugged green mountains down the middle, crowded plains along the coast, and white-capped Fuji standing alone south-west of Tokyo.
f: About three-quarters of Japan is mountainous, which is why its cities crowd onto the coastal plains.
The country has more than 100 active volcanoes.
A 2023 recount using digital maps found about 14,000 islands — twice the long-quoted figure of 6,852.

q.q: Roughly how much of Japan is mountainous?

Q85377.t: A frozen jigsaw at the top of North America
Q85377.s: Seen from above, this is a jigsaw of brown and white land fitted together with channels of sea ice. Tens of thousands of islands spread north of the Canadian mainland towards Greenland, and for much of the year the sea between them is frozen solid. Explorers spent centuries looking for a way through; the Northwest Passage threads these channels.
Q85377.w: Big, flat islands split by straight channels, white with sea ice most of the year; glaciers and ice caps in the east.
f: Three of the world's ten largest islands are here: Baffin, Victoria and Ellesmere.
Roald Amundsen was the first to sail the whole Northwest Passage, in 1903–1906.
More than 36,000 islands make up the archipelago.

q.q: Which sea route winds between these islands?

Q37394.t: Steep green islands where hundreds of languages are spoken
Q37394.s: Here the Pacific islands turn tall and green: steep volcanic ridges cloaked in rainforest and rimmed by reef, from New Guinea east to Fiji. Some volcanoes still smoke, so look for a grey plume drifting off a summit. Melanesia is also the most linguistically diverse corner of the planet — villages a few ridges apart can speak unrelated languages.
Q37394.w: Large, mountainous, forested islands with reef-fringed coasts; now and then a volcanic plume trailing downwind.
f: Papua New Guinea alone has more than 800 living languages.
Vanuatu has about 110 languages for some 300,000 people — the densest mix of languages per person on Earth.

q.q: Papua New Guinea alone has roughly how many languages?

Q3359409.t: Thousands of tiny islands above the deepest sea
Q3359409.s: Micronesia is mostly ocean: thousands of small islands, many of them low atolls whose rings of reef glow turquoise against deep blue. Many rise only a few metres above the waves. On its western edge lies the Mariana Trench, where the sea floor drops almost 11 km — about as far below the surface as a cruising airliner is above it.
Q3359409.w: Small rings of reef with pale-green lagoons, scattered far apart across dark-blue ocean; occasionally a higher, forested island.
f: The name means 'small islands' in Greek.
On Yap, huge stone discs called rai, some wider than a person is tall, served as money.

q.q: What does the name 'Micronesia' mean?

Q208643.t: The world's largest archipelago, where Asia meets Australia
Q208643.s: Between mainland Asia and Australia lies the largest group of islands on Earth — about 25,000 of them, from Sumatra to the Philippines. Look for chains of volcanic cones, rainforest cut into clearings, and shallow seas glowing green over coral. Alfred Russel Wallace travelled here for eight years and noticed that the animals on either side of a narrow strait belonged to different worlds.
Q208643.w: Big green islands and strings of volcanic peaks in warm, shallow seas; brown river plumes spreading into turquoise water.
f: The Wallace Line runs between Bali and Lombok, dividing mostly Asian wildlife to the west from Australian-type wildlife to the east.
While travelling in these islands in 1858, Wallace hit on natural selection independently of Darwin.

q.q: Between which two islands does the Wallace Line run?

Q38272.t: A green, cloud-dappled cluster off Europe's north-west edge
Q38272.s: Two large islands and thousands of small ones sit off the north-west coast of Europe, and on a clear day they look intensely green, patched with fields and fringed by rocky headlands. Cloud is common: Atlantic air brings frequent rain. Until roughly 8,000 years ago you could have walked here from the continent, across a plain now drowned beneath the North Sea.
Q38272.w: Great Britain's long north–south shape with Ireland to its west, a patchwork of green fields, and ragged island clusters in the north.
f: The group has more than 6,000 islands, most of them small and uninhabited.
The drowned land that once joined Britain to Europe is called Doggerland, after the Dogger Bank.
Warm water carried by the Gulf Stream keeps winters here mild for such a northern latitude.

q.q: What is the drowned land between Britain and Europe called?

Q664.t: One of the last large lands people reached
Q664.s: Two long islands and hundreds of small ones lie alone in the South Pacific, about 2,000 km east of Australia. Look for the snowy spine of the Southern Alps in the south and volcanic cones in the north. Polynesian voyagers arrived only about 700 years ago, making this one of the last large lands on Earth to be settled.
Q664.w: Snowy peaks in the south, glacier-blue lakes and fjords in the south-west, green farmland on the plains.
f: Cook Strait, between the two main islands, is only about 22 km wide at its narrowest.
New Zealand sits on Zealandia, a sunken continent that is about 94% under the sea.
Aotearoa, the Māori name, is often translated as 'land of the long white cloud'.

q.q: What is the Māori name for New Zealand?

Q3740828.t: Fire and ice on a rift in the Atlantic
Q3740828.s: Iceland looks unfinished from above: black lava fields and grey outwash plains, white ice caps, and a thin green rim along the coast. The island sits right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where North America and Eurasia pull apart, which is why it has so many volcanoes. Glacial rivers spread across the sand in braids, like pale veins.
Q3740828.w: Dazzling white ice caps inland, dark lava and sand plains, braided rivers and a narrow green strip by the sea.
f: The two plates move apart by about 2 cm a year, and Iceland slowly widens with them.
Vatnajökull, the largest ice cap, covers about 8% of the country and hides active volcanoes beneath it.
Geologists everywhere use the Icelandic word 'sandur' for a glacial outwash plain.

q.q: Which two plates pull apart across Iceland?

Q7463928.t: The Red Island, where life went its own way
Q7463928.s: Madagascar's nickname, the Red Island, makes sense from above: bare laterite soil shows through in rust and orange, and after rain the rivers pour red silt into the sea. It split from Africa, and later from India, tens of millions of years ago, and life here evolved in isolation. Look for green rainforest along the east coast and dry plains in the west.
Q7463928.w: A huge island with a green eastern escarpment, rust-red highlands, and rivers bleeding red sediment into the sea.
f: At about 587,000 km², it is the world's fourth-largest island.
Lemurs evolved only here, and about 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is found nowhere else.
Malagasy, the island's language, is closest to languages of southern Borneo, more than 6,000 km away.

q.q: Malagasy is most closely related to languages from which island?

Q710.t: A country of atolls in all four hemispheres
Q710.s: Kiribati is 33 tiny islands scattered across thousands of kilometres of ocean. From above, most are thin rings of land around pale lagoons, often only a few metres above the sea. It is the only country in all four hemispheres, and in 1995 it moved the date line so that all its islands share the same calendar day.
Q710.w: Thin rings of land enclosing jade-green lagoons, tiny against the deep blue, spread far apart along the equator.
f: 'Kiribati' is pronounced 'Kiribas' — the local form of 'Gilberts', the islands' old British name.
About half of the country's people live on South Tarawa, the capital atoll.

q.q: 'Kiribati' is the local form of which name?

Q192626.t: Volcanoes on a conveyor belt across the Pacific
Q192626.s: The islands line up from south-east to north-west, and their shapes tell the story. In the south-east the Big Island is broad and young, its volcanoes still active; further north-west the islands grow older, more eroded and more deeply cut by green valleys. Beyond them the chain dwindles into atolls and sunken seamounts. The chain was built as the Pacific Plate crept over a hotspot that stays put.
Q192626.w: A diagonal line of islands: broad dark volcanoes to the south-east, older, green, deeply furrowed islands to the north-west.
f: Hawaii is about 3,800 km from California, one of the most isolated island groups on Earth.
Kauai, near the north-western end of the main islands, is about 5 million years old; the Big Island is under 1 million.
A new volcano, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (formerly Lōʻihi), is growing on the sea floor south-east of the Big Island.

q.q: What created the Hawaiian Islands?
q.a: A hotspot under the Pacific Plate

Q234796.t: Where the new year arrives before anywhere else
Q234796.s: A loose line of coral atolls runs across the equator in the middle of the Pacific, hundreds of kilometres apart. The largest, Kiritimati, is hard to miss: a huge ring of land with a maze of shallow, milky-blue lagoons inside. The islands that belong to Kiribati keep time 14 hours ahead of Greenwich, so they greet each new year first.
Q234796.w: Tiny, isolated atolls strung north to south; Kiritimati stands out as a big pale ring full of patchy lagoons.
f: Kiritimati has the largest land area of any coral atoll, about 390 km².
Its name is the local spelling of 'Christmas': Captain Cook reached it on Christmas Eve 1777.
Of the 11 Line Islands, 8 belong to Kiribati; the rest are United States territories.

q.q: Which Line Island is the largest coral atoll by land area?

Q118350.t: Hundreds of atolls and a few high green islands
Q118350.s: The Carolines are scattered over some 3,000 km of the western Pacific, just north of the equator. Most are low atolls, rings of reef around turquoise lagoons, but Pohnpei, Kosrae and the peaks of Chuuk rise as green, cloud-capped islands. Their navigators crossed open ocean without instruments, and their knowledge helped revive Polynesian voyaging in the 1970s.
Q118350.w: Small turquoise-ringed atolls far apart; Chuuk shows as a huge reef ring with green peaks inside.
f: The islands are named after King Charles II of Spain.
Nan Madol, a town of basalt built on about 100 artificial islets off Pohnpei, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Master navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal guided the canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976.

q.q: Which king are the Caroline Islands named after?

Q165481.t: Four giant islands on a drowned edge of Asia
Q165481.s: Borneo, Sumatra, Java and Sulawesi make up the Greater Sunda Islands, and three of them rise from a shallow shelf that was dry land during the ice ages. The seas between them are rarely deeper than about 100 m, so the water often looks green rather than deep blue. Look for volcano chains along Sumatra and Java and dark rainforest on Borneo.
Q165481.w: Big green islands in shallow, greenish seas; lines of volcanic cones along Sumatra and Java.
f: Java is the world's most populous island, home to more than 150 million people.
In the ice ages people and animals could walk from mainland Asia to Java, Sumatra and Borneo.
Sulawesi is the odd one out: it lies beyond the Wallace Line and has a strange mix of wildlife.

q.q: Which is the largest of the Greater Sunda Islands?

Q1042.t: Granite islands left behind by a drifting continent
Q1042.s: Most islands in open ocean are volcanoes or coral, but the Seychelles' inner islands are granite — a sliver of an ancient continent, stranded when India drifted away to the north. From above, Mahé and Praslin show steep green hills and grey boulders tumbling into turquoise bays. Far to the south-west, the outer islands are flat coral atolls lost in the blue.
Q1042.w: Steep green granite islands with turquoise bays in the north-east; low, far-flung coral atolls to the south-west.
f: The coco de mer palm, native to Praslin and Curieuse, bears the heaviest seed of any plant.
Aldabra atoll is home to roughly 100,000 giant tortoises.
The Seychelles has the smallest population of any African country.

q.q: What rock are Mahé and Praslin made of?

Q4526612.t: A green teardrop off India's southern tip
Q4526612.s: Sri Lanka hangs off the tip of India like a teardrop, its narrow northern end pointing at a chain of sandbanks that almost reaches the mainland. The south-central highlands rise as a dark-green knot, with tea estates climbing their slopes. Around them lie rice paddies, reservoirs built by ancient kings, and a golden rim of beaches.
Q4526612.w: A teardrop-shaped island: mountains in the south-centre, and a thin chain of sandbanks reaching toward India from the north-west.
f: The word 'serendipity' comes from Serendip, an old name for the island.
Adam's Bridge, a chain of shoals about 50 km long, almost links Sri Lanka to India.
A footprint-shaped hollow on top of Adam's Peak is revered by Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians alike.

q.q: Which English word comes from an old name for Sri Lanka?

Q3593416.t: A heart-shaped island facing the Southern Ocean
Q3593416.s: Tasmania is shaped a little like a heart, and from above its west is wild: dark forest, buttongrass plains, jagged mountains and lakes, with hardly a road. The east is gentler, with farmland and white-sand bays. The next land to the south is Antarctica, and the westerlies of the Roaring Forties arrive straight off thousands of kilometres of open ocean.
Q3593416.w: A heart-shaped island south of Australia: rugged dark-green west, drier farmland and bright bays along the east coast.
f: Abel Tasman sighted it in 1642, and for two centuries it was called Van Diemen's Land.
Air measured at Cape Grim, on the north-west tip, is among the cleanest on Earth.
The Tasmanian devil now survives in the wild only here.

q.q: What was Tasmania's old European name?

Q40285.t: Rainforest, great rivers and ice beside the equator
Q40285.s: The world's second-largest island is a green giant with a mountain spine running its full length, usually wrapped in cloud. Rivers such as the Sepik and the Fly loop through swamp forest in wide brown meanders you can follow for hundreds of kilometres. In the west the peaks reach almost 4,900 m, high enough for small glaciers to have survived right beside the equator.
Q40285.w: A huge green island with a long, cloud-wrapped mountain spine and wide, snaking brown rivers through lowland swamp.
f: Puncak Jaya, 4,884 m, is the highest mountain on any island in the world.
At about 786,000 km², New Guinea is second only to Greenland among the world's islands.
Most of the world's birds-of-paradise, famous for their dancing males, are found on New Guinea.

q.q: Which is the highest peak on New Guinea?

Q36117.t: One island, three countries and a granite giant
Q36117.s: Borneo is the third-largest island on Earth, and from the air you can read its story in its textures. Deep, crinkled rainforest covers the interior, brown rivers coil towards the coast, and across many lowlands neat grids of oil-palm plantations have replaced the jungle. In the north-east, Mount Kinabalu's bare granite summit pokes above the clouds at 4,095 m.
Q36117.w: Dark rainforest, coiling brown rivers and geometric plantation grids; in the north-east, Kinabalu's rocky summit above the clouds.
f: Borneo is shared by three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei.
The Kapuas, about 1,140 km long, is Indonesia's longest river.
Wild orangutans live only on Borneo and Sumatra.

q.q: How many countries share the island of Borneo?

Q3492.t: Home of Toba, the world's largest volcanic lake
Q3492.s: Sumatra stretches almost 1,800 km across the equator, with a chain of volcanoes running down its western side. The unmissable landmark is Lake Toba: a blue oval about 100 km long, filling the crater of a supervolcano that erupted some 74,000 years ago. In its middle sits Samosir, nearly as big as Singapore — an island in a lake on an island.
Q3492.w: A long green island with a volcanic ridge along its west; look for Toba, a vast blue lake with a big island inside.
f: It is the only place where tigers, rhinos, orangutans and elephants still live side by side in the wild.
At about 473,000 km², Sumatra is the world's sixth-largest island.
The equator crosses Sumatra, so the island lies in both hemispheres.

q.q: What is the island in the middle of Lake Toba called?

Q13989.t: Fuji, the Japanese Alps and Tokyo on one long island
Q13989.s: Honshu is the long, bent heart of Japan, and from the window its variety is striking: snow on the Japanese Alps down the middle, rice plains and city sprawl along the coasts. On a clear day Fuji's lone white cone is unmistakable, south-west of Tokyo's vast grey-brown carpet. Tunnels and bridges tie Honshu to the other three main islands.
Q13989.w: A long curved island: snowy peaks down the centre, Fuji's solitary cone, and dense cities crowding the Pacific coast.
f: About 100 million people live on Honshu — more than on any island except Java.
At about 228,000 km², it is the world's seventh-largest island.
The Seikan Tunnel, which runs under the sea to Hokkaido, is about 54 km long.

q.q: Which island has more people than Honshu?

Q22890.t: The Emerald Isle lives up to its name
Q22890.s: On a clear day Ireland really is emerald: small fields in a hundred shades of green, stitched together by hedges and, in the west, by grey stone walls. The Atlantic coast is ragged with bays and headlands; the midlands are low, dotted with lakes and brown bog. Look for the River Shannon swelling into long lakes as it runs south towards the ocean.
Q22890.w: A green island west of Great Britain: ragged Atlantic coast, flat lake-dotted midlands and the long thread of the Shannon.
f: The Shannon, about 360 km long, is the longest river in Ireland or Britain.
Ireland has no native snakes: after the Ice Age the sea cut it off before they could arrive.
Lough Neagh, in the north-east, is the largest lake in the British Isles.

q.q: What is the longest river in Ireland?

Q23666.t: Europe's largest island, chalk cliffs to Highland lochs
Q23666.s: Great Britain runs almost 1,000 km from south to north, and flying along it you watch the land change. The south is a soft patchwork of fields and towns around London's huge sprawl; the Pennines form a brown spine through northern England; Scotland breaks up into mountains and long, narrow lochs. At night the cities blaze orange while the Highlands go almost dark.
Q23666.w: A long island narrowing northward: green farmland in the south, a brown upland spine, then Scotland's mountains and slender lochs.
f: It is the ninth-largest island in the world and the largest in Europe.
Ben Nevis, its highest mountain at 1,345 m, is still almost 10 km below cruising height.
The Channel Tunnel, about 50 km long, links it to France beneath the Strait of Dover.

q.q: What is Great Britain's highest mountain?

Q186233.t: A forested chain between the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea
Q186233.s: A narrow chain of islands, almost entirely cloaked in dark tropical forest, runs north to south between the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. It belongs to India but lies much closer to Myanmar. The water around it is exceptionally clear, so reefs show as pale turquoise halos. East of the main chain, tiny Barren Island is South Asia's only active volcano.
Q186233.w: A slim north–south chain of densely forested islands fringed by turquoise reef, with scattered small islets to the east.
f: Barren Island, only about 3 km across, is the sole confirmed active volcano in South Asia.
North Sentinel Island is home to one of the last peoples on Earth living without contact with the outside world.

q.q: Which active volcano lies in the Andaman Islands?

Q157286.t: Scattered green islands at the gateway to Malacca
Q157286.s: South of the Andamans, across the Ten Degree Channel, the Nicobars scatter in a loose line towards Sumatra. Some are flat coral islands ringed with palms; others, like Great Nicobar, are hilly and cloaked in rainforest. Most are closed to tourists to protect the Nicobarese and Shompen peoples, so the dark-green shapes and turquoise reefs are seen by few outsiders.
Q157286.w: A loose chain of islands between the Andamans and Sumatra: flat, palm-fringed ones in the north, hilly rainforest ones in the south.
f: The Ten Degree Channel, about 150 km wide, separates them from the Andamans along the 10th parallel.
The Nicobars lie far closer to Sumatra than to mainland India.

q.q: Which channel separates the Nicobars from the Andamans?

Q3827.s: For centuries these scattered islands were the world's only source of cloves and nutmeg, and ships sailed halfway round the globe to reach them. From above they are green cones and ridges rising steeply out of very deep blue water, their shores rimmed with coral. Ternate and Tidore, two volcanic cones facing each other across a narrow strait, are the classic view.
Q3827.w: Steep green volcanic islands and cones, rimmed with coral, rising from unusually dark-blue water.
f: Under a 1667 treaty the Dutch kept Run, a tiny nutmeg island here, and the English kept Manhattan.
Nutmeg and mace both come from the same fruit, native to the Banda Islands.
The Banda Sea plunges to more than 7 km deep in the Weber Deep.

q.q: Which spice came originally only from the Banda Islands?

Q119285.t: A 1,900-km arc of volcanoes reaching toward Asia
Q119285.s: Flights between North America and East Asia often skirt the Aleutians, a 1,900-km arc of volcanic islands trailing from Alaska towards Kamchatka. Fog and cloud hide them much of the time; when it clears, look for snow-streaked cones — Shishaldin on Unimak Island is one of the most symmetrical on Earth. North of the chain lies the Bering Sea, south of it the open Pacific.
Q119285.w: A long curving chain of rugged islands and snowy volcanic cones, often poking through a lid of fog.
f: The chain crosses the 180th meridian, so Alaska reaches into the Eastern Hemisphere.
The arc has dozens of volcanoes, and some erupt every few years.
The Unangan (Aleut) people have lived on these islands for about 9,000 years.

q.q: Which sea lies north of the Aleutian Islands?

Q216533.t: The top of Canada: ice caps, bare rock, almost no one
Q216533.s: At the northern edge of Canada lies a cluster of large islands with bare brown plateaus, glaciers spilling from ice caps, and channels choked with sea ice for most of the year. Only a few hundred people live here, in two small hamlets. The group was named in 1953 to mark the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.
Q216533.w: Big, flat-topped islands of bare rock, white ice caps and glaciers, separated by channels of pack ice.
f: Devon Island is the largest uninhabited island on Earth.
On Axel Heiberg Island, stumps of trees that grew about 45 million years ago still stand, preserved but not fossilised.
Scientists use Devon Island's Haughton impact crater to rehearse exploring Mars.

q.q: Which is the largest uninhabited island on Earth?

Q68740.t: Taller than Everest, if you start from the sea floor
Q68740.s: The Big Island is made of five volcanoes fused together, and from above you can see their broad, gentle domes and dark lava flows streaking down to the sea. Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa both top 4,100 m, and in winter their summits can be white with snow. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea is over 10,000 m tall — more than Everest.
Q68740.w: Two huge, gentle domes, snow-dusted in winter, with black lava flows running to the coast and perhaps a volcanic plume.
f: Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume.
Lava from Kīlauea has added new land to the island's south-east coast within recent decades.
The Big Island is larger than all the other Hawaiian islands combined.

q.q: How many volcanoes make up the island of Hawaii?

Q120755.t: Snowy Alps, turquoise lakes and fjords
Q120755.s: The Southern Alps run like a white wall down the length of the island, and on their dry eastern side glacial lakes glow an unreal milky turquoise — Tekapo and Pukaki are the brightest. To the west, glaciers tumble towards rainforest and the sea; in the south-west, Fiordland's drowned valleys cut deep into the mountains. East of the range, braided rivers fan across the Canterbury Plains.
Q120755.w: A white mountain wall down the island, vivid turquoise lakes on its eastern side, fjords slicing the south-west coast.
f: Aoraki / Mount Cook, 3,724 m, is New Zealand's highest mountain.
The lakes' colour comes from 'rock flour', fine silt ground by glaciers and suspended in the water.
At about 150,000 km², it is the world's 12th-largest island.

q.q: What gives South Island's glacial lakes their turquoise colour?

Q118863.t: Volcanoes, a caldera lake and a perfect lone cone
Q118863.s: The centre of the North Island is a volcanic plateau, and it shows. Lake Taupō, the country's largest lake, fills a caldera left by enormous eruptions; south of it rise Ruapehu, Tongariro and the neat cone of Ngauruhoe, often snow-capped. Out on the west coast, Taranaki stands alone: a near-perfect cone ringed by a sharp circle of forest amid green farmland.
Q118863.w: A large lake in the centre with snowy volcanoes to its south; on the west coast, a lone cone inside a circle of forest.
f: Lake Taupō, about 616 km², fills a volcanic caldera; its last great eruption was around 1,800 years ago.
About three-quarters of New Zealanders live on the North Island.
Auckland is built on a field of some 50 small volcanoes.

q.q: Which lake fills a volcanic caldera in the centre of the North Island?

Q709.t: Two chains of atolls, barely above the waves
Q709.s: The Marshalls are two parallel chains of coral atolls — the 'sunrise' and 'sunset' chains — strung across the central Pacific. From above, each atoll is a necklace of narrow islets around a lagoon, bright turquoise inside and deep blue outside. The land averages only about 2 m above sea level, so the islands can look like lines painted on the water.
Q709.w: Necklaces of thin islets around wide turquoise lagoons, lined up in two roughly parallel north-west to south-east chains.
f: Marshallese navigators made stick charts — frames of sticks and shells mapping the ocean swells around the islands.
The country has 29 atolls and 5 single islands, with only about 180 km² of land in all.

q.q: What did Marshallese navigators map with sticks and shells?

Q686.t: A chain of volcanoes, some of them still glowing
Q686.s: Vanuatu is a chain of about 80 islands running some 1,300 km north to south, and many of them are volcanoes. Steep green slopes drop to fringing reef, and in places bare ash plains and smoking craters break the forest. On Tanna, in the south, Mount Yasur has been erupting almost without pause for centuries; at night its crater glow can sometimes be seen from far away.
Q686.w: A long chain of green volcanic islands with reef edges; look for grey ash slopes and drifting plumes, especially in the south.
f: The land divers of Pentecost Island, who leap from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, inspired bungee jumping.
Vanuatu has an underwater post office, in the reef off Hideaway Island near Port Vila.

q.q: Which sport was inspired by Pentecost Island's land divers?

Q80389.t: A chain of volcanic cones stepping across the sea
Q80389.s: Between Kamchatka and Hokkaido the Kurils cross the sea like a line of stepping stones about 1,200 km long. Many are simply volcanoes poking out of the water, their slopes streaked with snow well into summer. Fog is the rule here, but on a clear day look for Alaid, a lone cone rising straight from the waves at the northern end of the chain.
Q80389.w: A line of small, steep volcanic islands and cones between two seas, often half hidden by fog.
f: Alaid, on Atlasov Island, rises to about 2,300 m and is the highest volcano in the chain.
On Onekotan, a volcanic cone rises from a lake that fills an older, larger crater.
Just offshore, the Kuril–Kamchatka Trench plunges more than 9 km deep.

q.q: Which sea lies to the west of the Kuril Islands?

Q1964385.t: Volcanic islands that are, officially, part of Tokyo
Q1964385.s: South of Tokyo Bay a thin line of volcanic islands runs more than 1,000 km out into the Pacific: first the Izu Islands, then the Ogasawara group, then the Volcano Islands. Many are single cones with steep, dark shores and a collar of white surf. However far they lie from the capital, all of them are governed by the Tokyo Metropolis.
Q1964385.w: A long north–south dotted line of small, steep volcanic islands, some with craters, fringed by white surf.
f: The Ogasawara Islands have never been joined to a continent, so many of their species live nowhere else; they are a UNESCO site.
Nishinoshima has grown many times over since eruptions began in 2013, swallowing the old island.
Ogasawara has no airport: the ferry from Tokyo takes about 24 hours.

q.q: Which city governs the Nanpō Islands?

Q11832316.t: Remote atolls of black pearls and empty lagoons
Q11832316.s: Far north of Rarotonga, a handful of small atolls lie scattered across hundreds of kilometres of ocean. From above they are classic rings: a thin rim of coconut palms around a lagoon that glows every shade from jade to turquoise. A few hundred people at most live on each inhabited island, and cultured black pearls from Manihiki's lagoon are the local treasure.
Q11832316.w: Isolated rings of land around jade and turquoise lagoons, widely scattered, with no high ground at all.
f: New Zealander Tom Neale lived alone on Suwarrow for years and wrote 'An Island to Oneself' about it.
Suwarrow is now a national park with no permanent residents, only seasonal caretakers.

q.q: What is Manihiki atoll famous for?

Q1011.t: Dry volcanic islands where Atlantic hurricanes are born
Q1011.s: Some 500 km off West Africa, ten volcanic islands rise from the Atlantic in shades of rust, ochre and grey — the Sahara's dry breath reaches this far. Sal and Boa Vista in the east are flat and sandy. In the south-west, Fogo is one enormous volcano, with a young black cone standing inside a broad, collapsed caldera.
Q1011.w: Brown, arid islands in deep-blue sea; Fogo is round, with a dark cone inside a caldera; the eastern islands are flat and sandy.
f: The islands were uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived around 1460.
Pico do Fogo, 2,829 m, is the highest point; it last erupted in 2014–15.
Many of the strongest Atlantic hurricanes begin as storms near these islands.

q.q: Which Cape Verde island is a single volcano with a cone inside its caldera?

Q891593.t: An island that was mapped as a peninsula until 1908
Q891593.s: At the mouth of the Khatanga Gulf, on the edge of the Laptev Sea, lies a low, roughly square island of tundra about 60 km across. For most of the year it is white and merges with the sea ice around it; in the short summer it turns brown-green and glitters with small lakes. Rivers run outwards from its central upland like the spokes of a wheel.
Q891593.w: A squarish, low tundra island at the mouth of a long gulf, lake-speckled in summer, often fused with sea ice.
f: Until 1908 it was mapped as a peninsula; Nikifor Begichev showed it was an island, and it now bears his name.
Its highest point, on the central Kiryaka upland, is under 200 m.
Begichev had earlier sailed on Eduard Toll's Russian polar expedition of 1900–1902.

q.q: What was Bolshoy Begichev thought to be before 1908?

Q219774.t: India's southernmost tip, wrapped in rainforest
Q219774.s: Great Nicobar is the largest and wildest of the Nicobars: hilly, almost wholly covered in rainforest, its rivers winding out through mangroves to the sea. Its southern tip, Indira Point, is the southernmost point of India, and Indonesia's Sumatra lies less than 200 km beyond it. The Shompen, a small forest people, live in the interior.
Q219774.w: A large, hilly, dark-green island at the southern end of the Nicobar chain, with pale beaches and mangrove creeks.
f: Much of the island is a biosphere reserve that includes two national parks.
Giant leatherback turtles come ashore on its beaches to nest.

q.q: What is Indira Point, on Great Nicobar, known for?

Q1473243.t: The Andamans' busy hub, ringed by reef and mangroves
Q1473243.s: Most flights to the Andamans land here, on the island that holds the capital and most of the islands' people. From the air South Andaman is a ragged shape of forested hills and deep, winding creeks lined with mangroves. Off its south-west coast, a marine national park protects reefs and a scatter of small islands set in pale turquoise water.
Q1473243.w: A ragged, hilly green island with long mangrove creeks; the town and airport on its east coast, small reef islands to the south-west.
f: The Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park, founded in 1983, covers some 15 small islands and their reefs.
Chidiya Tapu, at the island's southern tip, is known for its birdlife and sunsets over the sea.

q.q: Which marine national park lies off South Andaman?

Q222853.t: The largest Andaman island, forest from shore to shore
Q222853.s: Middle Andaman is the largest island of the chain, and from above it is almost unbroken forest from coast to coast. Its eastern shore is cut by long, branching creeks fringed with mangroves; the western side, facing the open sea, is wilder still and part of the Jarawa people's reserve. Look for small islands and turquoise reef patches off the east coast.
Q222853.w: An elongated island of near-continuous dark forest, with mangrove-lined creeks on the east and small islets offshore.
f: At about 1,500 km², it is the largest of the Andaman Islands.
Just to the south, on Baratang Island, small mud volcanoes bubble up through the forest.

q.q: What unusual feature is found on Baratang, just south of Middle Andaman?

Q2000510.t: The Andamans' highest peak rises from this forested isle
Q2000510.s: At the northern end of the Great Andaman chain, this island rises higher than any other: Saddle Peak, 732 m, stands near its east coast in a national park of dense forest. Around it, creeks and mangroves eat into the shore, and reefs trace pale lines offshore. Beyond, open sea stretches north towards Myanmar's Coco Islands.
Q2000510.w: The northernmost large island of the Andaman chain: forested hills rising to a high ridge near the east coast.
f: Saddle Peak, 732 m, is the highest point of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Off Diglipur, the little islands of Ross and Smith are joined by a narrow sandbar, making a pair of twins.

q.q: What is the highest point of the Andaman Islands?

Q82601.t: Magellan's 'Land of Fire' at the bottom of the Americas
Q82601.s: At the very tip of South America the Andes bend east and crumble into islands, glaciers and fjords. The main island of Tierra del Fuego is two landscapes in one: flat, tawny steppe with pale lakes in the north, and snowy mountains with glaciers spilling towards the sea in the south. The Strait of Magellan cuts it off from the mainland.
Q82601.w: A big triangular island: yellow-brown plains in the north, snowy peaks and glaciers in the south, the Beagle Channel along its southern edge.
f: Magellan named it in 1520 after the fires he saw burning along its shores.
Cape Horn lies on a small island at the archipelago's southern edge.
The Beagle Channel is named after HMS Beagle, the ship that later carried Charles Darwin here.

q.q: Which strait separates Tierra del Fuego from the mainland?

Q1952.t: Almost an island, hugged by the world's highest tides
Q1952.s: Nova Scotia is a long peninsula tied to the mainland only by a narrow neck of land, and nowhere in it is more than about 67 km from the sea. The Atlantic coast is a ragged fringe of coves, rocks and islets. On the north-west side, the Bay of Fundy has the highest tides in the world: at low water, look for vast red mudflats where there was sea a few hours before.
Q1952.w: A long peninsula parallel to the mainland, a deeply indented Atlantic coast, and reddish tidal flats along the Bay of Fundy.
f: Fundy's tides can rise and fall by about 16 m, the greatest range on Earth.
The name is Latin for 'New Scotland'.
Sable Island, a thin crescent of sand far out in the Atlantic off Nova Scotia, is home to wild horses.

q.q: Which bay beside Nova Scotia has the world's highest tides?

Q170479.t: A mountainous island between the ocean and the mainland
Q170479.s: Vancouver Island runs about 460 km along Canada's Pacific coast, its spine of snowy mountains dividing two worlds. The west side faces the open ocean with deep sounds, surf and temperate rainforest; the sheltered east side has farmland and towns along the Strait of Georgia. At its southern tip is Victoria, capital of British Columbia — the city of Vancouver is across the water on the mainland.
Q170479.w: A long mountainous island parallel to the coast: snowy peaks down the middle, fjord-like inlets on the ocean side.
f: It is the largest island on the Pacific coast of North America.
Its highest peak, the Golden Hinde, reaches 2,195 m.
It is named after George Vancouver, who charted this coast in 1792.

q.q: Which capital city stands on Vancouver Island?

Q158129.t: A jagged Arctic giant riddled with lakes
Q158129.s: Victoria Island is the eighth-largest island in the world, and one of the oddest-looking: its coast splays into long peninsulas and deep bays like a spilled blot of ink. Inland, the low tundra is spattered with countless lakes that stay frozen for much of the year. Only about 2,000 people live here, mostly in Cambridge Bay and Ulukhaktok.
Q158129.w: A huge, low, ragged island with spreading peninsulas, deep bays and tundra freckled with lakes, often under sea ice.
f: At about 217,000 km², it is bigger than Great Britain.
The border between Nunavut and the Northwest Territories runs across it.
It holds the largest known island in a lake on an island in a lake on an island.

q.q: Victoria Island is larger than which of these islands?

Q380307.t: A wild, lake-spattered land where icebergs drift south
Q380307.s: Labrador is the wild mainland half of Newfoundland and Labrador: a rocky plateau scoured by ice-age glaciers and spattered with thousands of lakes. In the north the Torngat Mountains rise in sharp peaks straight from the sea, with small glaciers tucked into their hollows. Offshore, the cold Labrador Current carries icebergs south from Greenland in spring and early summer.
Q380307.w: Barren rocky upland dotted with countless lakes, a fjorded coast and sharp peaks in the north; icebergs offshore in spring.
f: Mount Caubvick in the Torngats, 1,652 m, is the highest point of mainland Canada east of the Rockies.
The shimmering gemstone labradorite is named after this region.
Norse sagas mention a forested 'Markland', which many historians place here.

q.q: Which gemstone takes its name from Labrador?

Q146841.t: Canada's northern tip, under 800 km from the Pole
Q146841.s: Ellesmere is the northernmost part of Canada, and from above it looks as if the Ice Age never quite ended: ice caps and glaciers pour through dark mountains into fjords sealed with sea ice. Its northern tip, Cape Columbia, is less than 800 km from the North Pole. Only around 150 people live here, most of them in the Inuit hamlet of Grise Fiord.
Q146841.w: Dark mountains buried in ice caps, glaciers spilling into fjords, and frozen sea on every side.
f: Alert, on its north-east coast, is the northernmost permanently staffed place on Earth.
Barbeau Peak, 2,616 m, is the highest point in Nunavut.
Fossils of Tiktaalik, a fish with limb-like fins, were found here in 2004.

q.q: What is the northernmost permanently staffed place on Earth?

Q81178.t: The world's fifth-largest island, cut by fjords and ice
Q81178.s: On polar routes between Europe and western North America you may cross Baffin, Canada's biggest island. Its east coast is dramatic: mountains, ice caps and deep fjords walled with granite, often edged by sea ice or icebergs. The west is lower and flatter, dotted with lakes. Iqaluit, the capital of Nunavut, sits at the head of Frobisher Bay in the south-east.
Q81178.w: A huge island with a mountainous, fjord-slashed, ice-capped east coast and low, lake-dotted tundra to the west.
f: At about 507,000 km², Baffin is Canada's largest island and the fifth-largest in the world.
Mount Thor's sheer granite face, about 1,250 m high, is the world's greatest vertical drop.
Norse sagas describe a stony 'Helluland', usually identified with Baffin.

q.q: Which territorial capital is on Baffin Island?

Q48335.t: The Rock, where Vikings landed a thousand years ago
Q48335.s: Transatlantic flights often make landfall over Newfoundland, a big, rugged island of rock, bog, forest and countless ponds. Its coast is a maze of long bays and headlands, and in spring icebergs from Greenland drift past. Near its northern tip, around the year 1000, Norse sailors built a small settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows — the only confirmed Viking site in North America outside Greenland.
Q48335.w: A big, rough-edged island of dark forest and bog, speckled with ponds, its coast a maze of deep bays.
f: Newfoundland keeps its own time zone, half an hour ahead of Atlantic time.
In Gros Morne National Park, the Tablelands expose rock from the Earth's mantle.
Cape Spear, near St. John's, is the easternmost point of North America outside Greenland.

q.q: What is the Norse site near Newfoundland's northern tip called?

Q3812.t: The island shaped like a sprawling letter K
Q3812.s: Sulawesi is instantly recognisable on a map and from the air: four long, mountainous arms reach out from a central knot, so nowhere is very far from the sea. Deep gulfs lie between the arms, and inland the ridges hide clear, deep lakes. The island sits beyond the Wallace Line, and many of its animals, like the tusked babirusa pig, live nowhere else.
Q3812.w: Four long, narrow, mountainous peninsulas spreading from a centre like a starfish, with deep gulfs between them.
f: Lake Matano, about 590 m deep, is the deepest lake in South-East Asia.
In the highlands of Tana Toraja, traditional houses carry huge upswept roofs shaped like boats.
At about 180,000 km², Sulawesi is the world's 11th-largest island.

q.q: Which letter is Sulawesi's outline often compared to?

Q3757.t: A string of volcanoes on the world's most crowded island
Q3757.s: Java is about 1,000 km long, and down its spine marches a line of volcanic cones, many of them active — on a clear day you can count them one after another. Between them, rice fields and towns fill every valley: more than 150 million people live here. In the east, look for the Tengger caldera, a grey 'sea of sand' with the smoking crater of Bromo inside.
Q3757.w: A long island with a row of volcanic cones along its length; in the east, a grey sandy caldera holding smaller cones.
f: Semeru, 3,676 m, is Java's highest volcano and one of its most active.
At night Java glows almost from end to end with the lights of its towns and cities.
Borobudur, in central Java, is the largest Buddhist temple in the world.

q.q: Which is Java's highest volcano?

Q124873.t: Mount Apo, rare eagles and a 10-km-deep trench offshore
Q124873.s: Mindanao, the Philippines' big southern island, is a sprawling, many-armed shape of forested mountains, volcanoes and wide river plains. Near Davao, Mount Apo rises to 2,954 m, the highest point in the country. Just off the east coast the sea floor drops into the Philippine Trench, more than 10 km deep — nearly as far down as a cruising airliner is up.
Q124873.w: A large, many-lobed island of green mountains and plains, with a big lake on its north-central plateau and Mount Apo near Davao.
f: Lake Lanao, on the north-central plateau, is the second-largest lake in the Philippines.
Mindanao's forests are the last stronghold of the Philippine eagle, one of the largest eagles in the world.
It is the second-largest island in the Philippines, after Luzon.

q.q: What is the highest mountain in the Philippines?

Q125384.t: Mayon's perfect cone and a volcano inside a lake
Q125384.s: Luzon is the largest island of the Philippines: a long shape with a mountain spine in the north and a ragged tail curling to the south-east. Look south of Manila's sprawl for two lakes — broad Laguna de Bay, and Taal, with a volcanic island in its middle. Near the south-eastern tip stands Mayon, a cone so symmetrical it looks drawn with a ruler.
Q125384.w: Mountains in the north, Manila's sprawl around its bay, two big lakes to the south, and a lone perfect cone near the south-eastern tip.
f: Mayon, 2,462 m, is famous as one of the most perfectly shaped volcanic cones on Earth.
Laguna de Bay, just south-east of Manila, is the largest lake in the Philippines.
The rice terraces of the Cordillera, in northern Luzon, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which lake near Manila has a volcanic island in its middle?

Q22502.t: Mountains higher than Fuji on a leaf-shaped island
Q22502.s: Taiwan is shaped like a leaf, and its two sides could hardly be more different. The east is a wall of mountains dropping almost straight into the Pacific, with more than 200 peaks above 3,000 m. The west slopes gently down to a crowded plain of cities and fields that blazes with light at night. The Tropic of Cancer runs across the middle.
Q22502.w: A leaf-shaped island: steep forested mountains packed along the east, a busy flat plain along the west coast.
f: Yushan, or Jade Mountain, reaches 3,952 m — higher than Mount Fuji.
Portuguese sailors called it Ilha Formosa, 'beautiful island'.
Sun Moon Lake, in the central mountains, is the island's largest body of water.

q.q: What does 'Formosa', an old name for Taiwan, mean?

Q13987.t: Where volcanoes smoke above the city streets
Q13987.s: Kyushu, the southernmost of Japan's main islands, is volcano country. In its centre, Aso's caldera is so vast that towns, farms and a railway fit inside it. In the south, Sakurajima rises from Kagoshima Bay just across the water from the city, often trailing a plume of ash. The coast is ragged with bays and islands, especially towards Nagasaki in the west.
Q13987.w: A mountainous island with a huge round caldera in its middle and a smoking volcano in a southern bay.
f: The name Kyushu means 'nine provinces', after its old divisions.
During Japan's long isolation, the islet of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour was its only window for European traders.
Aso's caldera measures roughly 25 by 18 km.

q.q: What does the name Kyushu mean?

Q13991.s: Shikoku is the smallest and least crowded of Japan's four main islands, mostly steep, forested mountains with towns strung along the coast. To the north lies the Seto Inland Sea, calm water studded with islands and crossed by long bridges. In the Naruto Strait, on the east side, the turning tide spins whirlpools that can reach about 20 m across.
Q13991.w: A compact mountainous island south of the island-dotted Seto Inland Sea, linked to Honshu by long bridges.
f: Pilgrims walk a circuit of 88 Buddhist temples around the island, about 1,200 km in all.
Mount Ishizuchi, 1,982 m, is the highest peak in western Japan.
Three bridge routes link Shikoku to Honshu across the Seto Inland Sea.

q.q: How many temples are on Shikoku's famous pilgrimage?

Q35581.t: Japan's snowy north, where sea ice reaches the shore
Q35581.s: Hokkaido feels different from the rest of Japan: wider fields, bigger forests, fewer people and far more snow. From above, look for round caldera lakes — Shikotsu, Tōya, Kussharo — set among volcanic hills. In late winter, drift ice from the Sea of Okhotsk packs against the north-east coast and the Shiretoko Peninsula, turning the sea white.
Q35581.w: A big island of broad farmland, forested mountains and round blue caldera lakes; white in winter, with sea ice along the north-east.
f: The Shiretoko Peninsula in the north-east has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2005.
It covers over a fifth of Japan's land but holds only about 4% of its people.
Sapporo hosted the Winter Olympics in 1972.

q.q: Which indigenous people have their homeland on Hokkaido?

Q7792.t: A long, thin island almost touching the mainland
Q7792.s: Sakhalin stretches nearly 950 km from north to south but is never more than about 160 km wide — from the air it looks like a long green-and-brown fish. Two mountain ranges run along it with a valley in between. In the north-west, the Nevelskoy Strait narrows to about 7 km from the mainland, and in winter it freezes right across.
Q7792.w: A very long, narrow island parallel to the coast, with two mountain ridges and a central valley; icy seas in winter.
f: It is Russia's largest island, at about 76,000 km².
Anton Chekhov travelled here in 1890 and wrote the book 'Sakhalin Island'.
At its southern tip, La Pérouse Strait separates Sakhalin from Hokkaido by about 40 km.

q.q: Which writer travelled to Sakhalin in 1890 and wrote a book about it?

Q1462.t: Emerald coves and 7,000 ancient stone towers
Q1462.s: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean, a rugged block of hills and plateaus with surprisingly few towns. Watch the coast: in the north-east, the Costa Smeralda's granite coves glow emerald and turquoise, while long white beaches line the south. Just to the north, across a narrow strait, Corsica rises much higher.
Q1462.w: A large, roughly rectangular island with a rugged interior; bright turquoise coves in the north-east and Corsica just to the north.
f: Some 7,000 nuraghi — Bronze Age stone towers — are scattered across the island.
The mountain villages of Ogliastra are famous for an unusually high number of people living past 100.
The Strait of Bonifacio, only about 11 km wide, separates Sardinia from Corsica.

q.q: What are Sardinia's ancient stone towers called?

Q14112.t: A mountain range rising straight from the sea
Q14112.s: The French call Corsica 'the mountain in the sea', and from above you see why: a jagged granite range fills almost the whole island, streaked with snow well into spring and rising to 2,706 m. The west coast is a run of deep gulfs and red cliffs; the east is a flatter strip of lagoons. At the northern tip, the thin finger of Cap Corse points towards Genoa.
Q14112.w: A mountainous island with a finger-like peninsula pointing north; deep gulfs on the west coast, flat lagoons on the east.
f: Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio, on the west coast, in 1769.
The GR20 trail along Corsica's mountain spine is often called Europe's toughest long-distance hike.
The red cliffs of Scandola, on the Gulf of Porto, are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which emperor was born on Corsica?

Q4951156.t: A triangular island crowned by smoking Etna
Q4951156.s: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean, a rough triangle that earned it the ancient name Trinacria. Its landmark is unmissable: Etna, a broad, dark volcano on the east coast, snow-capped in winter and often trailing a plume. To the north, look for the Aeolian Islands, where Stromboli has been throwing up small bursts of lava for thousands of years.
Q4951156.w: A triangular island; on its east coast, Etna's huge dark cone, often with a plume; small volcanic islands to the north.
f: Etna, about 3,300 m, is the tallest active volcano in Europe, and its height changes with its eruptions.
The Strait of Messina separates Sicily from mainland Italy by only about 3 km.
Stromboli's regular glowing bursts earned it the nickname 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'.

q.q: Which ancient name for Sicily refers to its shape?

Q337524.t: Vanuatu's biggest island, once taken for a continent
Q337524.s: Espiritu Santo is the largest island of Vanuatu: a rugged, forested west side rising to the country's highest peaks, and a lower east side of plantations, reefs and white beaches. In 1606 the navigator Pedro Fernández de Quirós landed here and believed he had found the great southern continent. Look for turquoise reef flats along its eastern shores.
Q337524.w: A large green island with a high mountain wall along its west side and flatter, reef-fringed shores to the east.
f: Mount Tabwemasana, 1,879 m, is the highest point in Vanuatu.
Spring-fed 'blue holes' in its eastern forest are pools of startlingly clear, bright-blue water.

q.q: What did Quirós believe Espiritu Santo was in 1606?

Q148966.t: A double chain of jungle islands and vast lagoons
Q148966.s: The Solomons form two long, roughly parallel chains of high, jungle-covered islands with a sheltered sea between them. Their coasts are fringed by reefs and mangroves, and in the west the Marovo Lagoon spreads as a maze of islets and turquoise channels. Far to the south, Rennell is a raised coral atoll with a huge lake where its lagoon used to be.
Q148966.w: Two parallel lines of mountainous, dark-green islands, fringed by reef, with a turquoise maze of lagoon in the west.
f: The Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña named the islands in 1568, hoping they held King Solomon's riches.
Lake Tegano on Rennell Island is the largest lake in the insular Pacific.
On Malaita, strings of shell money are still used for bride price and ceremonies.

q.q: Whose legendary wealth inspired the name of the Solomon Islands?

Q10905515.t: A 1,000-km arc of coral seas from Kyushu to Taiwan
Q10905515.s: South-west of Kyushu, the Ryukyus trail away in a long arc towards Taiwan, each island ringed by coral reef and water in a dozen shades of blue. Okinawa, the largest, is long and narrow, with busy towns in the south and green hills in the north. For more than four centuries these islands were the independent Ryukyu Kingdom, trading between Japan, China and South-East Asia.
Q10905515.w: A long chain of small islands wrapped in bright turquoise reef, stretching south-west from Kyushu towards Taiwan.
f: Karate grew up in Okinawa, from local martial arts blended with Chinese influences.
The Iriomote cat, one of the rarest wild cats on Earth, lives on a single island here.
From Yonaguni, the westernmost island, Taiwan is only about 110 km away.

q.q: Which martial art originated in Okinawa?

Q183963.t: The world's largest chain of atolls
Q183963.s: The Tuamotus scatter nearly 80 coral atolls across a vast stretch of the South Pacific — the largest group of atolls on Earth. From above, each is a thin, broken ring of palm-topped land around a lagoon of luminous turquoise, with deep blue all around. The biggest, Rangiroa, is so wide that from one shore of its lagoon you cannot see the other.
Q183963.w: Dozens of thin, broken rings of land around glowing turquoise lagoons, strewn across dark-blue ocean.
f: Early navigators called them the 'Dangerous Archipelago', because the low atolls were so hard to spot.
Rangiroa's lagoon covers about 1,450 km², one of the largest in the world.
Much of French Polynesia's famous black-pearl farming takes place in Tuamotu lagoons.

q.q: What did early European navigators call the Tuamotus?

Q154628.t: A broken ring of volcanic islands off New Guinea
Q154628.s: The Bismarck Archipelago curves around the Bismarck Sea like a broken ring. New Britain is the big crescent, mountainous and smoking in places; New Ireland is its long, skinny neighbour; Manus and the Admiralty Islands lie to the north-west. At New Britain's north-eastern tip, look for Rabaul, a town built around a flooded volcanic caldera.
Q154628.w: A big crescent island with volcanic peaks, a long thin island to its north-east, and scattered smaller islands.
f: The islands were named in 1884 after the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck.
New Ireland is about 350 km long but in places less than 10 km wide.
Rabaul's harbour fills a caldera whose volcanoes, such as Tavurvur, still erupt.

q.q: Who is the Bismarck Archipelago named after?

Q201766.t: Smoking volcanoes on an explorer's namesake island
Q201766.s: Bougainville is a big, mountainous island draped in rainforest, with a chain of volcanoes down its spine. Mount Balbi is the highest, at about 2,700 m, while its neighbour Bagana is one of the most active volcanoes in the region, often trailing a plume of steam and ash. The coasts are lined with reef, black-sand beaches and mangroves.
Q201766.w: A long mountainous island of dark rainforest with volcanic peaks down the middle, often with a plume drifting from one of them.
f: It is named after the French explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville, who sailed past in 1768.
The bright bougainvillea flower is named after the same explorer.
Geographically, it is the largest island of the Solomon Islands chain.

q.q: Which garden plant shares its name with this island's explorer?

Q192767.t: Jungle peaks on one side, grassy plains on the other
Q192767.s: Guadalcanal is the largest island of the Solomon Islands, and strikingly lopsided. A wall of jungle-covered mountains, rising to more than 2,300 m, runs along its southern side, where the rainy 'Weather Coast' drops steeply to the sea. The north is gentler, with grassy plains, plantations and the national capital, Honiara.
Q192767.w: A long island with steep, cloud-capped mountains along the south coast and pale grassy plains along the north.
f: It is named after Guadalcanal in Andalusia, the home town of a member of Mendaña's Spanish expedition of 1568.
The south coast is called the Weather Coast for its heavy rain and rough seas.

q.q: Which city on Guadalcanal is the capital of Solomon Islands?

Q83639.t: Six volcanoes fused into a seahorse on the equator
Q83639.s: Isabela, the largest of the Galápagos, is made of six shield volcanoes that have grown together, and from above its outline looks like a seahorse. Broad, dark lava flows streak their flanks, and several summits hold vast calderas. The equator crosses its northern end, yet Galápagos penguins fish in the cold currents along its shores.
Q83639.w: A seahorse-shaped island of broad, dark volcanoes with huge summit craters and black lava flows running down to the sea.
f: Wolf volcano, 1,707 m, is the highest point in the Galápagos.
The pink iguana lives on the slopes of Wolf volcano and nowhere else on Earth.
Sierra Negra's summit caldera measures about 7 by 10 km.

q.q: What shape is Isabela Island often compared to?

Q42000.t: A figure eight of green peaks inside a reef
Q42000.s: Tahiti is two old volcanoes joined by a narrow neck, so from above it looks like a figure eight: big, round Tahiti Nui and smaller Tahiti Iti. Their slopes are sliced into deep green valleys that run from cloud-wrapped peaks down to beaches of black sand. A reef encircles much of the island, holding a pale turquoise lagoon inside.
Q42000.w: A large round island joined to a smaller one by a thin isthmus: knife-edge green ridges, a turquoise lagoon and a white line of surf.
f: Mount Orohena, 2,241 m, is the highest point in French Polynesia.
Captain Cook came here in 1769 to observe Venus crossing the face of the Sun.
The surf break at Teahupo'o hosted the Olympic surfing contest in 2024.

q.q: What did Captain Cook come to Tahiti to observe in 1769?

Q188705.t: The Valley Isle, crowned by Haleakalā's vast crater
Q188705.s: Maui is two volcanoes joined by a low isthmus, which earned it the name the Valley Isle. The big eastern one, Haleakalā, rises to 3,055 m, and its summit holds an enormous depression dotted with rust- and ochre-coloured cinder cones, easy to pick out on a clear day. The older West Maui Mountains are carved into sharp green ridges and valleys.
Q188705.w: Two lumps joined by a flat neck: the huge, often cloud-ringed dome of Haleakalā to the east, sharp green ridges to the west.
f: Haleakalā's summit depression is about 11 km long and 800 m deep.
In winter, humpback whales gather to breed in the channels between Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi.
Haleakalā means 'house of the sun' in Hawaiian.

q.q: What does 'Haleakalā' mean in Hawaiian?

Q208198.t: Fiji's main island: lush in the east, golden in the west
Q208198.s: Viti Levu is the largest island of Fiji, roughly round, with rugged forested mountains in the middle. The weather splits it in two: the south-east, around Suva, catches the trade-wind rain and stays dark green, while the drier north-west is a patchwork of sugar-cane fields and pale grassland. Coral reefs and lagoons fringe much of the coast.
Q208198.w: A roundish, mountainous island: dark rainforest in the south-east, paler golden cane country in the north-west, reefs along the shore.
f: Mount Tomanivi, 1,324 m, is the highest point in Fiji.
The Sigatoka Sand Dunes on the south coast became Fiji's first national park.
Most international flights to Fiji land at Nadi, on the island's dry western side.

q.q: Which city on Viti Levu is Fiji's capital?

Q205695.t: Home of the dodo, and an 'underwater waterfall'
Q205695.s: Three volcanic islands lie in a line east of Madagascar: Réunion, Mauritius and little Rodrigues. Réunion is the tallest and wildest, its highest peak topping 3,000 m, with one of the world's most active volcanoes on its south-east side. Mauritius is lower and ringed by a turquoise lagoon; off its south-west corner, sand pouring down an undersea slope looks from the air like a waterfall.
Q205695.w: Réunion's high, round, cloud-capped peaks; lower Mauritius to the north-east, wrapped in a wide turquoise lagoon.
f: The islands are named after the Portuguese navigator Pedro Mascarenhas.
The dodo, a flightless pigeon, lived only on Mauritius and was extinct by the late 1600s.
Piton des Neiges on Réunion, 3,069 m, is the highest point in the Indian Ocean.

q.q: On which island did the dodo live?

Q192281.t: The last large land to be put on the world map
Q192281.s: Severnaya Zemlya was the last sizeable land on Earth to be discovered: a Russian expedition sighted it in 1913, and it was not properly mapped until 1930–32. From above it is a cluster of big islands where smooth ice caps cover about half the land, their edges calving into the sea, and the rest is bare brown polar desert. Sea ice locks it in for most of the year.
Q192281.w: Big islands under smooth white ice domes, bare brown ground at their edges and frozen straits between, north of the Taymyr Peninsula.
f: The Academy of Sciences Ice Cap on Komsomolets Island is the largest ice cap in Russia.
Georgy Ushakov and Nikolay Urvantsev mapped the archipelago by dog sled in 1930–32.
Cape Arktichesky, its northern tip, is a common starting point for North Pole expeditions.

q.q: In which year was Severnaya Zemlya discovered?

Q1249802.t: Windswept, treeless islands full of penguins
Q1249802.s: Two main islands and hundreds of small ones lie in the South Atlantic east of Patagonia: low, treeless and brown-green under a big sky. The coast is torn into long inlets and sounds. Look for pale streaks on the hillsides — these are stone runs, rivers of boulders left by ice-age frost. Along the shores live huge colonies of penguins and albatrosses.
Q1249802.w: Two large, low, treeless islands with deeply indented coasts and pale streaks of boulder fields on the hills.
f: Five species of penguin breed here, including king, gentoo and rockhopper penguins.
About 70% of the world's black-browed albatrosses nest on these islands.
There are no native trees; the land is covered in grass, heath and peat.

q.q: What are the Falklands' 'stone runs'?

Q25231.t: Pointed mountains, flowing glaciers and a vault of seeds
Q25231.s: Svalbard is where the Arctic looks most dramatic from the air: dark, sharp-crested mountains, glaciers flowing between them like frozen rivers, and ice fronts calving into fjords. Around 60% of the land lies under ice. Willem Barentsz named the main island Spitsbergen — 'pointed mountains' — when he sighted it in 1596.
Q25231.w: Jagged dark peaks separated by broad white glaciers, fjords ending in ice cliffs, and sea ice to the north and east.
f: Longyearbyen is the northernmost town on Earth with more than 1,000 inhabitants.
The Global Seed Vault, dug into a mountain near Longyearbyen, stores seeds from all over the world.
The midnight sun shines here from about late April to late August.

q.q: What does the name 'Spitsbergen' mean?

Q185018.t: Europe's northernmost islands, locked in pack ice
Q185018.s: Franz Josef Land is a scatter of nearly 200 islands high in the Arctic, most of them buried under ice caps, with dark basalt cliffs showing at their edges. From above the ice domes look smooth and rounded, and the channels between them stay frozen for much of the year. Cape Fligely on Rudolf Island is the northernmost point of Europe, about 900 km from the Pole.
Q185018.w: Dozens of islands under smooth, rounded ice caps, with dark cliffs at their edges and frozen channels between them.
f: An Austro-Hungarian expedition discovered the islands in 1873 and named them after Emperor Franz Joseph.
Fridtjof Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen spent the winter of 1895–96 here in a stone hut.
Champ Island is famous for its strange, almost perfectly round stone balls.

q.q: Which emperor gave his name to Franz Josef Land?

Q80413.t: A 1,000-km wall of ice and rock between two seas
Q80413.s: Novaya Zemlya is a long, curved barrier, nearly 1,000 km from end to end, dividing the Barents Sea from the Kara Sea — the Ural Mountains carried on out into the Arctic. Its two main islands are separated by the narrow Matochkin Shar strait. The southern one is tundra and bare hills; the northern one is largely buried under a vast ice cap whose glaciers break off into the sea.
Q80413.w: A very long, narrow, curving pair of islands: brown tundra in the south, a continuous white ice cap in the north.
f: The northern island's ice cap, about 20,000 km², is one of the largest in Europe.
Willem Barentsz and his crew spent the winter of 1596–97 near its northern tip, in a hut of driftwood.
Matochkin Shar, the strait between the two main islands, is about 100 km long.

q.q: Which two seas does Novaya Zemlya separate?

Q3803.t: Volcano after volcano, from Bali to Timor
Q3803.s: East of Java the islands grow smaller and drier — Bali, Lombok, Sumbawa, Flores and on towards Timor — and most are crowned by volcanoes. Some peaks hold striking crater lakes: Rinjani on Lombok cradles a blue crescent of water with a young cone rising inside it. Farther east, green gives way to brown savanna, where Komodo dragons still roam a few islands.
Q3803.w: A west–east chain of volcanic islands, greener in the west and browner in the east; look for crater lakes and calderas.
f: On Flores, the three crater lakes of Kelimutu each have a different colour, and the colours shift over time.
Tambora, on Sumbawa, was left with a caldera about 6 km wide by its great eruption of 1815.
Remains of Homo floresiensis, a tiny extinct human nicknamed the 'hobbit', were found on Flores in 2003.

q.q: Which Lesser Sunda island has three crater lakes of different colours?

Q215664.t: Hundreds of reefs scattered across the South China Sea
Q215664.s: Across the southern South China Sea lie well over a hundred reefs, atolls and sandy cays, many of them awash at high tide. From above they appear as faint turquoise smudges and pale rings on deep blue, with only a few specks of real land among them. Old British charts marked this whole area with a blunt warning: 'Dangerous Ground'.
Q215664.w: Faint turquoise rings and patches of reef strewn across dark-blue sea, with very little dry land.
f: The islands are named after Richard Spratly, a British whaling captain who sighted one of them in 1843.
All their natural dry land put together covers only about 2 km².

q.q: How did old British charts label the Spratly area?

Q201012.t: Arctic islands made of ice, sand and mammoth bones
Q201012.s: The New Siberian Islands lie low and flat between the Laptev and East Siberian seas, often impossible to tell apart from the sea ice around them. In summer they show as brown tundra and grey sand, with lakes and crumbling cliffs of ancient ground ice. The frozen soil holds so many mammoth bones and tusks that ivory hunters have come here for more than two centuries.
Q201012.w: Low, flat, brown and grey islands with many lakes, blending into the surrounding sea ice for much of the year.
f: Bunge Land, between Kotelny and Faddeyevsky islands, is a low sandy plain that floods during storms.
In 1811 Yakov Sannikov reported a mysterious land to the north; 'Sannikov Land' was never found.
Kotelny is the largest island of the group.

q.q: Which phantom land was reported north of the New Siberian Islands?

Q128011.t: The Caribbean's big islands, from Cuba to Puerto Rico
Q128011.s: The Greater Antilles are the heavyweights of the Caribbean: Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, lined up from west to east. From above they are large, green and mountainous, edged by pale sand and turquoise shallows, while the Atlantic to the north falls away to deep, dark blue. Cuba, the largest, stretches some 1,200 km from end to end.
Q128011.w: A west–east line of big green islands: long, narrow Cuba, then mountainous Hispaniola, with Jamaica to the south and Puerto Rico last.
f: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, at about 105,000 km².
North of Puerto Rico, the Puerto Rico Trench plunges to about 8,400 m, the deepest point of the Atlantic.
Jamaica's Blue Mountains, rising to about 2,250 m, gave their name to a famous coffee.

q.q: Which is the largest island in the Caribbean?

Q21713615.t: Turquoise banks so bright they seem lit from below
Q21713615.s: In the Bahamas the water steals the show. The islands sit on vast limestone banks only a few metres deep, which glow an almost unreal turquoise, rippled with sand patterns. Cutting into the Great Bahama Bank is the Tongue of the Ocean, a deep trench whose ink-blue water ends abruptly against the pale shallows — one of the sharpest colour lines you will see from a plane.
Q21713615.w: Huge areas of glowing pale-turquoise shallows with sandy ripples, low islands along their edges, and sharp lines where deep blue begins.
f: Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here, in October 1492.
The country counts about 700 islands and more than 2,000 small cays.
Dean's Blue Hole, off Long Island, drops about 200 m, one of the deepest known.

q.q: In which year did Columbus make his first landfall in the Bahamas?

Q93259.t: A curved necklace of islands closing off the Caribbean
Q93259.s: The Lesser Antilles curve for some 800 km from the Virgin Islands down to Grenada, dividing the Caribbean from the Atlantic. Most are steep, green volcanic islands, each a peak with a skirt of reef; Guadeloupe is shaped like a butterfly. On a clear day, look on Saint Lucia's west coast for the Pitons, two sharp volcanic spires standing side by side at the water's edge.
Q93259.w: A curving chain of small, steep, green volcanic islands running north to south, with the open Atlantic to the east.
f: The inner islands are volcanic; outer ones such as Antigua and Barbados are flatter and made of limestone.
Kick 'em Jenny, north of Grenada, is an active volcano still growing beneath the sea.
The Pitons of Saint Lucia are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

q.q: Which island is famous for two volcanic spires called the Pitons?

Q59771.t: A crescent of rainforest and steep volcanic cones
Q59771.s: New Britain is a long, curving crescent about 500 km from end to end, the largest island of the Bismarck Archipelago. Along its north coast stands a line of volcanoes; the most striking is Ulawun, a steep, symmetrical cone that is also one of the most active in Papua New Guinea. Inland, the limestone Nakanai Mountains hide giant sinkholes and underground rivers.
Q59771.w: A long crescent-shaped island of dark rainforest with volcanic cones along its north coast, one of them tall and symmetrical.
f: Ulawun, about 2,300 m, is one of the Decade Volcanoes chosen for special study.
It is Papua New Guinea's largest island after New Guinea itself.
Some sinkholes in the Nakanai Mountains are hundreds of metres deep.

q.q: Which active volcano stands on New Britain's north coast?

Q17044696.t: The country that gave the world the word 'atoll'
Q17044696.s: The Maldives look like turquoise beads scattered on dark-blue velvet: 26 atolls in a double chain some 870 km long, each a ring of reefs and tiny islands around a pale lagoon. Many islands are just a strip of white sand and palms holding a single resort or village. The capital, Malé, fills its small island edge to edge with buildings.
Q17044696.w: Rings of pale-turquoise reef and dots of white sand on deep-blue ocean, arranged in a long north–south double chain.
f: 'Atoll' comes from 'atholhu', a word in Dhivehi, the Maldivian language.
The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country: its natural ground rises only about 2.4 m at most.
The country has about 1,200 coral islands, fewer than 200 of them inhabited.

q.q: Which English word comes from the Maldivian language?

Q25263.t: Green volcanic islands in the middle of the Atlantic
Q25263.s: Nine volcanic islands lie scattered across the mid-Atlantic, about 1,500 km west of Lisbon. From above they are intensely green, patched with small fields, with lakes lying in old craters. The unmistakable one is Pico: a near-perfect cone 2,351 m high, Portugal's tallest mountain, whose summit often pokes out above a sea of cloud.
Q25263.w: Small green islands in open ocean; a single tall dark cone on Pico, and round crater lakes on São Miguel.
f: The Azores sit where the Eurasian, North American and African plates meet.
In the Sete Cidades caldera on São Miguel, two joined lakes show different colours — one blue, one green.
The Azores High, a zone of high pressure named after the islands, shapes much of Europe's summer weather.

q.q: What is the highest mountain in Portugal?

Q6980542.t: An island you can barely tell from the ice around it
Q6980542.s: Along the coast of West Antarctica, the Getz Ice Shelf holds a string of islands locked into its floating ice. Wright Island, about 65 km long, is one of them. Completely buried under ice, it shows only as a broad, gentle swell above the flat shelf, easiest to spot when a low sun casts shadows. To the north lies the Amundsen Sea, often choked with sea ice.
Q6980542.w: A long, smooth white swell rising slightly above the flat ice shelf, with ice-covered sea to the north.
f: It was first mapped from air photos taken during the US Navy's Operation Highjump in January 1947.
It is named after Admiral Jerauld Wright, in overall command of Operation Deep Freeze in 1957–58.
The Getz Ice Shelf, which holds the island, stretches for more than 500 km along the coast.

q.q: Which ice shelf holds Wright Island?

Q1543171.t: An ice island found by an icebreaker in 1962
Q1543171.s: Grant Island is one of several islands frozen into the Getz Ice Shelf off Marie Byrd Land, in West Antarctica. About 37 km long and wholly ice-covered, it is hemmed in by the shelf on every side except the north, where a strait opens towards the sea. From above it is a smooth white hump, its outline given away mainly by shading along its slopes.
Q1543171.w: A smooth white hump rising from the flat ice shelf, with a strait of open water or sea ice along its northern side.
f: Sailors aboard the icebreaker USS Glacier discovered and charted it on 4 February 1962.
It is named after Commander E. G. Grant, the ship's captain at the time.
The smaller Shepard Island lies only about 9 km to the west.

q.q: Which ship's crew discovered Grant Island in 1962?

Q6272638.t: A lonely ice island off the Ruppert Coast
Q6272638.s: On the Ruppert Coast of Marie Byrd Land, far from any regular flight path, the Nickerson Ice Shelf holds a handful of ice-covered islands. Newman Island is about 28 km long and completely buried. From above it looks less like an island than a low, rounded bulge in the ice, with glaciers flowing down from the mainland to the south.
Q6272638.w: A low, rounded white bulge within a flat ice shelf, with glaciers descending from the land to the south.
f: It was mapped from US surveys and Navy air photographs taken between 1959 and 1965.
It is named after Commander J. F. Newman of the US Navy, who served on Operation Deep Freeze in 1966.

q.q: Which ice shelf holds Newman Island?
